utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Judge Thelin is not able to sit today, but we expect that he will be able to sit from Monday. There's a second issue that has arisen. It will be necessary for us to alter the normal timetable this morning a little. We will sit for two sessions of one hour, 40 minutes, which is longer than we normally extend, and we will have one 20-minute break. That will reach us to 1.00, and it will then be necessary for us to adjourn for the day. Done that way, we will lose only 25 minutes of sitting time and it should not affect Mr. Lukic or Mr. Bulatovic, because they're first up this morning, and the -- I am afraid it is just necessary that there be a break at that time. People may have noticed that I am sitting in two other cases with two other Judges this afternoon, and much must be done before 2.15. So we will go one hour, 40, have a 20-minute break; one hour, 40, and that, if my sums are correct, will get us to 1.00. Good morning, sir. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, that still applies. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. With the Court's permission, may Mr. Theunens sit us with this morning, from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see no objection, and it's our normal custom with experts, yes. Any other issue? Mr. Lukic, I believe you have a little problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that you make this offer, I just wanted to check in with something. We filed a motion with the Chamber yesterday for our expert report to be allowed seven days later in relation to how it was originally planned. Our report is rather lengthy; it runs into about 100 pages. We've tried to organise something with the translation service of the Tribunal, but they seem to be snowed under right now with their work, so we have sent the report to Belgrade for translation, which should be completed one of these days. I know now that Mr. Weiner does not oppose a later submission of this report. Mr. Vuga, if, indeed, he is to appear in this case, will be our last witness and this will leave us with plenty of time for the OTP to familiarise themselves with the expert report. You remember that during the summer he drafted an additional expert report, because certain aspects of the OTP's expert witnesses' accounts needed supplementing. We have received word from Belgrade that the report is nearing completion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Moore had some comments on this and I tried to get him this morning, but he was in transit, and I would be able to contact him during the break and just see what his comments were on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Weiner, the Chamber can deal with the matter now, even if we assume there was objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Personally, I don't see any objection to it, because schedule-wise we can move it towards the end and we will still have sufficient time to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have a week extra, Mr. Lukic. Now, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now that we've started raising procedural matters, I'm not sure if I should raise this issue now or at the end of today. It's about the next witness and the Chamber's order. We have received all our medical files, and if this is something that the Chamber wishes to deal with now, I think it might be a good idea to go into private session. It is a sensitive issue. Or perhaps we best just leave it for the end of today. I'm not sure what fits our schedule better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the sounds of it, it is a little more detailed than the matters we've mentioned so far, so hopefully we will have three or four minutes at the end of the day before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters can't hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have to speak up, Mr. Bulatovic. Your microphone is pointing away from you, almost.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not reaching the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter still can't hear Counsel Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. Carry on, Mr. Bulatovic. Just speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm doing my best, Your Honours, but it seems that the equipment isn't working properly. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we're hearing the interpretation clearly. Carry on. Just assume that we don't have any microphones here and you are determined that Mr. Weiner will hear every word you say. So speak to Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jaksic, please bear in mind the caution, yesterday's caution, about the way we talk. Try to comply with our -- there were certain problems yesterday. You were speeding with your answers. Please wait for me to complete my question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to keep my questions short and clear. Please try to answer the same way, and I hope we can finish up soon.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I heard yesterday that you said that your direct superior in October, 1991, was Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said there were daily briefings with Mr. Mrksic that you went to and daily briefings at the headquarters of the 1st Assault Detachment; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to briefings with Mr. Mrksic where we were given operative assignments. Major Tesic was there with me. At the headquarters of the 1st Assault Detachment, it was us who gave out assignments to company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any assignments from Mr. Mrksic, any orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive these orders orally or in a written form?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the orders were transmitted orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a single order signed by Mr. Mrksic, a written order, in relation to the Petrova Gora TO unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: These reports that you submitted, the briefings, were these written reports or did you report orally?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports were oral. However, at these briefings, I had my notebook which I made notes in, and then I would pass these notes on to the company commanders orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Orders that you got from the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, Major Tesic, were those written or oral?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters was in the same house, the headquarters of the 1st Assault Detachment and the headquarters of the Petrova Gora TO unit. So we were working closely together and we talked a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing about the transcript. Page 5 -- all right, okay, there's been a correction. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The orders which you handed out to your company commanders, did you do that orally or did you submit written orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During combat operations, things were happening at such a mad pace, there was simply no time for orders to be written down. So orders were passed on orally or over radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After briefings at the operations group headquarters and after receiving your assignments, which you later passed on to the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment, did you have any observations to make, although that's no military term, about these orders that you received; something about possibly amending these orders, supplementing these orders, reporting to your superior about amendments or revisions to orders, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no amendments, no revisions. On the 3rd, I had to stretch the entire Petrova Gora detachment along the line that was twice the length of the previous one, all the way up to Leva Supoderica. But I did not raise any objections. I believe that to be normal, as Mr. Mrksic had said. The TO men were familiar with the area and they should be in front of the guards battalion. They knew every house, every yard, and I understood that it was necessary for them to act as our scouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, if you could just please slow down slightly for the benefit of the record. Can we then agree that what seems to follow from this is that Mr. Mrksic had accurate knowledge of the situation on the ground, that his orders were proper and that he enjoyed a great deal of authority as a commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to an issue that is of great interest to us. I'm talking about the government meeting in Vukovar on the 20th of November. You did hint at that yesterday, didn't you? I want to know when you got to Velepromet in Vukovar on that day, the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Vukovar throughout. I would shuttle between the headquarters, Velepromet, and the operations group south command. I was going back and forth between these three places all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly yesterday, you had no official post at the time. Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time. I wasn't involved in the attack on Milovo Brdo. On the 17th of November, I attended a meeting at which decisions were taken as to what would be done after the liberation of Vukovar, which steps would be taken; what to do with the TO units later on. The idea was to discuss -- to have the police man check-points to control the flow of citizens. Vukovar was all in ruins and Velepromet was still standing. So all the towns' institutions were to be based there, since that neighbourhood was less destroyed than others. We had to set up a court. We had to set up medical facilities. We had to help mend the Vuteks facilities, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how it was that you were informed about the arrival of representatives of the SAO Krajina cabinet, Slavonia, Baranja, and western Srem? How did you know they would be arriving on that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not been informed. It was just by chance that I met Milos Vojinovic Dragan, and he was the one who told me that the cabinet members would be, would be arriving with Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript, page 8, line 2. It says "Sljivancanin" and it should read "Vojinovic".

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Jaksic, what time it was when you eventually reached Velepromet? And did your meeting with Vojinovic, the chance meeting that you had, occur in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was as they were arriving. We met there at about noon, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Before you went to see Mr. Mrksic, which is something we'll discuss later on, in addition to Mr. Vojinovic, did you discuss this issue with any other member of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was when you went to see Mr. Mrksic? By this time, you remember that it was about noon that you spoke to Mr. Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just after. Just after this conversation. I'm not sure if I met Goran again later on. I'm not sure if that was before or after. But I went to see Mr. Mrksic to tell him about this and to inform him of these various positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When did you return to Velepromet, having visited Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't stay with Mr. Mrksic for too long. I just told him about this. He was quite determined. He said there was no way the civilians could be left to the TO. And I simply went straight back to tell them about Mr. Mrksic's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking is: You remember it was at about noon that you spoke to Vojinovic. Can you tell me how much later you returned to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at about noon, give or take an hour or two. It is very difficult to be specific. This was, after all, 15 years ago. I can hardly remember what I had for lunch yesterday. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This meeting at Velepromet, did it begin after you had already returned from seeing Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. One thing I do know is I didn't attend the entire meeting, and I wasn't there for the opening statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who opened the meeting? When you say you weren't there for the meeting's opening, that implies that you actually do know that there was an opening speech that was made. Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the meeting took, the cabinet meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay through the entire meeting, until the very end?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The footage that Mr. Mrksic's Defence showed you yesterday, if you can remember some of the frames, the atmosphere that prevailed at the meeting and everything, was this footage taken after the meeting or before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before the meeting, when Goran Hadzic and Dokmanovic and the delegation of the Jagodina municipality arrived, and they congratulated us on liberating Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was your official capacity at that meeting? Why were you there, since you say that they congratulated you on liberating Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just me, all the people of Vukovar, all the citizens present there. And I happened to be there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: What was your official capacity, the capacity in which you attended that meeting, since we know that you did not have an official position at the time. You had withdrawn from the army, from politics. You were no longer into that. So I want to know: What was the official reason for you being there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dokmanovic and Goran Hadzic knew exactly what I had done and where I had been, and for as long as I had an official capacity, we would meet. And they appreciated my work, so that was the only reason that I had been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: About this meeting, you say you don't remember who opened the meeting, but you know that someone did. Did anyone in particular chair the meeting? Was there a chairman? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I wasn't there at the opening speech. I didn't know what the subject was. I didn't know what they were going to talk about, so that's why I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that he was there, I believe, Serb, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You can't remember him being in the hall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw footage that showed him with Goran, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in what capacity Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was present in Velopromet on that day with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was accompanying Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that you had contact with Hadzic while you held the position that you held. Was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, always with Mr. Hadzic when you met him and saw him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you surprised to see Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, at the meeting and in Velepromet on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me why you weren't surprised, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan provided security for Mr. Badza. It was the TO of the Operative Group North. I saw him there a couple of times. I wasn't particularly surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me who Badza is. Could you explain this for the Chamber and for us. Perhaps the Prosecution doesn't know who this person is. Tell us who Badza is.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all called this person Badza; that was his nickname. Radovan Stojkovic, Stajkovic, something like that. I don't know what his exact name is. I think it was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, you were with him.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I only met the commander over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This person Radovan Stojkovic, Badza, what position did he hold in Vukovar? You mentioned some Territorial Defence force. I'm interested in knowing what position he had.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Operative Group North TO, with its headquarters in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether at the meeting held on the 20th of November there was someone from the command of the Operative Group North who was present?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which members of the government were present in Velepromet on the 20th of November. You've seen footage. You've been reminded of this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Vojinovic, Rade Leskovac, Goran Hadzic, Slavko Dokmanovic. I can't remember all of the others exactly. I can't remember the names and surnames. I didn't really know them before the war either, so it is difficult for me to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Boris Bugunovic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Boris Bugunovic? Who was he in the government? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Boris Bugunovic is from Negoslavci. As for the position he held within the government, I couldn't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that he was the Minister of Internal Affairs, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really, because I didn't cooperate with him later. I cooperated with the people who formed the unit, who were trying to find facilities to establish a police station. I didn't cooperate with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were commander of the Petrova Gora TO, did you cooperate with Bugunovic during that period?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you see him in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him in Daja, Negoslavci, Sid, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the circumstances under which you would see him? Did you see him privately, officially? Were you assigned a task of some kind when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just would bump into each other. We would greet each other. We didn't go into lengthy discussions. We hadn't known each other before the war, we hadn't socialized, so we weren't really that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you this again: Do you remember this meeting which everyone is interested in? Or can you remember whether the conclusions of any kind were adopted at that meeting? Did the government adopt conclusions of any kind at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I spoke to Goran Hadzic and he said: "Jaksic, let's move from a military administration to a civilian government in Vukovar. Let's do that as soon as possible. Use your authority so that Milos Bibic could be the president of the executive board," once this government had been established. I can remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We heard that before this meeting you saw Mr. Mrksic with regard to the request that you had mentioned. Did you inform Goran Hadzic about the requests submitted to you, that you went to see Mrksic and you informed him Goran Hadzic about the results of the conversation with Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Mrksic, was anyone else present while you had this conversation that concerned the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is always some of the officers in the command. I can't remember exactly who was there, though. I was only interested in Mr. Mrksic. I had direct contact with him. If he can remember who was there, he can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Colonel Mrksic about the identity of the person who had sent you there to discuss this subject?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Mrksic, or did you perhaps come to such a conclusion on the basis of your conversation with him, did you tell him that in Vukovar, in Velepromet, there were members of the government of the SAO Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When speaking to Mr. Bugunovic [as interpreted], did you come to the conclusion that you should inform members of the government about your conversation with Mr. Mrksic, about the outcome of your conversation with Mr. Mrksic, the members of the government who were present in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There is no evidence of him speaking to Mr. Bugunovic at that meeting. The question is: "When speaking to Mr. Bugunovic, did you come to the conclusion that you should inform members ..." There was no evidence that I am aware of that he spoke with Mr. Bugunovic at that meeting. In fact, I believe he said he didn't see him at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He certainly didn't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to intervene. I was preempted. There is an error in the transcript. It should say Vojinovic, not Bugunovic. This translation error, this interpretation error, has provoked such a reaction on the part of the Prosecution. I didn't mention Bugunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're entirely innocent. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Mrksic had returned, I've already asked you whether you spoke to Mr. Hadzic about this. Did you tell anyone else, apart from Vojinovic, and I'm referring to the members of the government who were present, did you tell anyone else about the outcome of your conversation with Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Vojinovic is a member of the government, and if I informed him of this, it's as if I had informed the government. It wasn't necessary to inform anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how Mr. Vojinovic reacted when you informed him of the outcome of your conversation with Mr. Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How did you react when Mr. Mrksic told you that what you wanted was not possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite normally, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You can't remember the contents of the meeting, the conclusions, the course that the session followed. But I would like to know whether you can remember whether this subject was mentioned at the session of the government, the subject of POWs.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details, but I believe that there was something, that there was some tension in the army as far as the subject of prisoners is concerned. But I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This tension with regard to the army that you have mentioned, do you know what it consisted of, what the source was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an intervention with regard to a bad interpretation. Page 16, line 7, it says that the tension is within the army, but the witness said that the tension was exerted on the army, which is quite different. If necessary, I will try to clarify what is at stake with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, explain something for all of us here: Pressure exerted on the army, what does this mean exactly? Tension against the army, what does this mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was to make the military administration transform into a civilian government, and in part it had to do with the prisoners. I can't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So this pressure exerted on the army, this tension on the army, with regard to the POWs, can you remember any of the details? Can you explain to us what was at stake? Who was exerting pressure on whom, and for what reasons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who was exerting pressure, but it was all within that context. They wanted to put criminals in Krajina on trial so that they wouldn't cross over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who participated in the discussions at that session, at that meeting that the government held?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there very briefly. It wasn't my duty. I wasn't obliged to attend, so I really wasn't trying to remember the details. This happened 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were there briefly. Can you remember how much time you spent, in total, at the government session? Does the name Bogdan Mujic Vujic mean anything to you -- Bogdan Vujic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't meet him. I think he's some official, someone from the security organ, but I never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I showed a photograph to you taken from the film that we saw yesterday --?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the leave of the Trial Chamber, if we could show this photograph which has been taken from that film, from that footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps that would refresh your memory. Can we have a look at that photograph. That's part of Exhibit 269.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've never had any contact with this person, nor have I ever spoken to him. I can't remember this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, I never claimed that you had had contact with him.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult, because everyone was in uniform. It's difficult to recognise people in uniform; they all look the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you can remember having seen this person at the government session.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember because I didn't know him, and as a result I didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person in the photograph is Mr. Bogdan Vujic. This is Exhibit 269. It concerns the events of the 20th of November, 1991, at 1405 hours. With the leave of the Trial Chamber, could this photograph be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this photograph will be Exhibit 771.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, could we agree that after you had spoken to Mr. Vojinovic about the subject that you spoke about, you then went to see Mr. Mrksic with your request because, in your opinion, given everything that you knew about Mr. Mrksic and given the fact that he had the position that he had, he was the person who had the authority to grant your request.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic was the immediate superior; that was my belief. As to whether he was competent, whether he had such authority, I didn't think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you go to see Mr. Mrksic if you believed that he had no such authority? Or did you go to see him because you thought he had such authority?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're playing with words. I contacted the immediate superior. There is a hierarchy within the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a reserve captain, he finished an officer school in Bilaca, and if Mr. Mrksic told you that this wasn't possible, do you know who Mr. Mrksic's superior was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't try to find anything out about the subordination. I assumed that it was the General Staff, but I really wasn't interested in the structure and the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Mrksic was essential for you, given the situation in the field, and that is why you contacted him; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that session ended, can you remember where you went? Did you go somewhere with Goran Hadzic, if I remember what you said correctly yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then went to Petrova Gora with Goran Hadzic. Behind his vehicle there was Slavko Dokmanovic with his group. Slavko Dokmanovic. By the clinic, the turning for Petrova Gora, there was automatic fire opened up from a number of weapons. As I'm used to that, naturally we continued. Mr. Dokmanovic's vehicle almost ended up in a ditch, perhaps because they were afraid. It stopped. We headed on, continued towards Petrova Gora, then I noticed that Dokmanovic didn't follow us. We went to Petrova Gora, walked around Petrova Gora, saw the people. It was late in the afternoon. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether, at the end of this meeting, Mr. Hadzic gave an interview in the yard of Velepromet? Did he give an interview for some TV station?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the footage, in the photograph, it was possible to see him giving an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see Mr. Hadzic giving any interviews on television? Did you ever see him doing that? He was the prime minister. You were close to him.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember watching quite a lot of interviews, but I can't remember the details. I wasn't interested in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have an exhibit marked for identification; 576 is the number of the exhibit. Could we see it, please. The transcripts of the interview, for the B/C/S version of the transcript, the number is 3D000214; the English version is 3D000215. Could we see the English version on the screen for the Trial Chamber, and could we see this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, please follow the interview. Listen to what Mr. Hadzic says, and then I will have a number of questions for you, if you can be of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if you were able to follow the transcript of the interview in English, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "No" is the short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an exhibit in the Dokmanovic trial, 205, Exhibit 205 in the Dokmanovic trial, and the relevant transcripts are all available. We shall be submitting extra copies to you during the break, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just carry on, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, have you seen this interview by Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you first saw this interview in relation to the government meeting that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me about now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you now have --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it is getting dark here. Petrova Gora and Vukovar had no electricity. We didn't have electricity, we didn't have TV, we had nothing. How could I possibly have seen it at the time. This interview was given in Sid that afternoon. But we certainly weren't able to follow these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this interview, this footage before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You did see a video yesterday with Mr. Hadzic, and now you see him again. Was this his physical appearance on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a uniform back then, and the same applies to this footage. He has this black closely-cropped beard, and the cap. So nothing changed in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You've heard this interview now, haven't you? You see that it tallies with the reason that you went to see Mr. Mrksic for, in order to establish a judiciary, in order to establish judicial bodies and proper authorities, that sort of thing. Mr. Jaksic, can we agree that the issue of POWs was discussed at the government meeting, and how conclusions were reached that Mr. Hadzic addressed in this interview; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were tensions about the army, but I don't remember any details, because it was, after all, a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to phrase it this way: Do you think Mr. Hadzic would really have said this for the record had it not been established previously at the government meeting, and knowing what Mr. Hadzic was like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Weiner, I was raising an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will defer to the Court, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's pure conjecture. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek that the Hadzic interview be admitted into evidence. It was already exhibited in the Dokmanovic trial, so I expect no particular opposition from the OTP on that count. And the same applies to the relevant transcript, which we shall be submitting copies of during the next break. But copies are available on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this matter be -- could be left pending until after the break until we get a chance to review the transcripts and see what exactly was said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the moment, as I understand it, we have the film marked for identification only and we have no transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. But we should receive it sometime during the break, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The issue will be held for a while, Mr. Bulatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, if I remember correctly yesterday, you said that Velepromet was the TO headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The staff, not the headquarters, that's what I said. For mobilisation purposes; the archive was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Marko Crevar mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Ljubenko Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who was this person?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the protection platoon securing Velepromet, the Trend factory, the brick factory, the winery, and all the other facilities that had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You probably mentioned a person named me Milan Bibic or Rajko Bibic in your testimony, didn't you? Correct me if I'm wrong, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rajko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the name of Milan Bibic? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Bibic might, not Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This Bibic, and I may have been misinformed about the name, does he have anything to do with the Negoslavci [Realtime transcript read in error "Yugoslav"] TO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's a reserve officer, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a correction for the transcript. I think it is quite material. On page 23, line 22, we have Yugoslav TO, whereas the reference was to the Negoslavci TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend for this intervention. That's page 23, line 22, it should read "Negoslavci TO", not "Yugoslav TO".

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic I asked you about your relationship with Milos Bibic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to do staff drills together before the war, and that's where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But I asked you about your relationship. How was your relationship? Good? Bad?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mile Uzelac as the man who, together with Slobodan Grahovac, had arrived from Sid with you to set up the TO units. How come you knew Mile Uzelac? And what was your relationship?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, another intervention. Page 24, line 12, it should Mile Uzelac. I have no idea what this is supposed to be, what I see on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milo Uzelac was a teacher of mine in secondary school, a math teacher for about a year, and later on he was the Chief of Staff of the Vukovar municipality TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And your relationship?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Darko Fot in your evidence, didn't you? Darko Fot, did he occupy a position in Vukovar's TO staff? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war but not during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which specific position, his position in the TO after the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujevic was a commander with him at the staff, but I don't know exactly what he was doing. I had switched over to traffic by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go a step back, sir. It is my mistake, really. Was the then TO commander, Mr. Miroljub Vujevic, at the government meeting that we spoke about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of Darko Fot, do you know who appointed him to any position at all within the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about what went on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to another question. It's about your removal. I heard yesterday that Mr. Sljivancanin told you about the decision to replace you at the headquarters of the 1st Assault Detachment; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who else was there when he told you about this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroljub, myself, and Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You're a reserve officer, aren't you? You completed an elite college for reserve officers, didn't you? Orders removing an officer from a position of command, is this something that is normally just shared orally like that, or is this something that needs to be written down?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime, orders, be they oral, be they written, all carry the same weight and all have the same importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you seek any sort of explanation from Mr. Sljivancanin when he told you about this, or perhaps an explanation from Mr. Tesic, or perhaps from Mr. Mrksic? Was any sort of explanation provided to you as to why you were no longer allowed to keep that position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed on in Vukovar for about a month, a month and a half. I had been in Vukovar for over one and a half years. By this time, with all the tension and all the pressure, I was worn out and tired. I just wanted to go back to my peaceful life, I wanted to go back to my business, I wanted to go back to being a family man, and I did not wish to remain a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You had been suffering a lot under all the pressure and tension for a long time. You were fed up and you wanted out. So this was a convenient way out for you. Before Mr. Sljivancanin informed you of this, had you previously made any complaints to anyone? Had you told anyone about being fed up and about wanting to leave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mrksic was at the Operation Staff. Mr. Sljivancanin spent all of his time with his unit up and about. The commander and the security organ had the power.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, my question was: Did you ever complain to anyone that you were fed up with everything and that you just wanted out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned something that you described as the Vietnam syndrome yesterday. You said you began to feel this develop. How did that reflect on the way you carried out these assignments? How did it start to show, in your case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt it right at the beginning, when the Guards Brigade first came in. Those lads who were there for 10 or 15 minutes, they just passed outside the command briefly, but you immediately became very close with them, as though they were family. Several hours later, they come back in body bags or maimed, back from the front line. It is a horrible thing. Once you've seen all of that - your neighbours, your friends, your fellow soldiers getting maimed or killed - it all comes back to you after a while and you begin to recede, you begin to withdraw. It does work that way and it does affect your mental state. I lost many people from my company. I lost many of my relatives. I lost many of my family. So it all comes to a head at the end and it simply affects you in a bad way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it exactly what you are now talking about that affects the quality of your command? Wouldn't be it normal for something like that to affect the quality of one's command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The worst tensions were at staff meetings in Ralik and Velepromet. You can't do two things at the same time. If you're over at the staff, it's your command that suffers, and vice versa. In wartime conditions, it was the commander that took care of everything, and everything had to be done quickly. Civilian life, military life, the economy, everything just had to be dealt with swiftly, and very soon the exertion became too much. If I'd only had to deal with one thing, maybe I could have coped, but they wanted me everywhere. The villages, the TO, the Vukovar people, those evacuating and the mobilisation, if you add all of that up, it was getting too much for me. And if it hadn't been like that, it would have been far easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you ask for them to replace you? Why didn't you contact Mrksic, Mr. Tesic, and say, "I can't carry on"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been logical for Commander Mrksic to ask me to come see him and to speak to me. However, there were other matters at stake. Mr. Sljivancanin contacted Miroljub immediately. It was the Montenegrin connection, and they were in contact from the very beginning. And from the very beginning, he had some sort of negative feeling towards others. With the Brcanska Brigade I cooperated well. If he had said, "Go to Dunav," if he had said, "Go to Dunav," even if I couldn't swim, I would have gone. But Sljivancanin was arrogant and there was no particular form of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, do you know that a written order was issued to relieve you as commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there's a written order about appointing Darko Fot to a position in the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I immediately moved over to the traffic organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, were you the subject of processing by the security organ because it was thought that you were involved in smuggling cars, weapons, et cetera? Were you ever the subject of such investigations? I'm only interested in you saying "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what hurt me the most, as an honest man, because the acts of others were attributed to me. Those who were involved in those acts -- well, we soon came to see who had earned money, who had made a lot of money. After the war, I had lost ten times as much as they had gained. You can see what kind of processing was involved, what sort of investigations were involved. When I told the chief of the SUP that, I asked him: Is it possible for something like this to have been told to an honest man? If I had had money in the bank, it could have been checked. I was driving a Yugo vehicle. It was a Serb's vehicle and I returned it to him. I didn't have any profit from the war. I didn't have profit of any kind. I was poorer than I had been. This was Mr. Sljivancanin's problem, in that criminals were appointed and honourable men were dismissed. That's a huge error. That's why he's here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, do you know that Boro Bugunovic had been investigated in this way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in the security issues involved in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is information, according to which Boro Bugunovic sold weapons to local people for a price between 800 and 1.000 German marks? Have you heard anything of this kind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bought a pistol for 700 and it wasn't even totally functional, but not from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is information, according to which, Mile Uzenac was removing evidence and that's why it wasn't possible to mobilise staff, the TO? There was such evidence in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the state appointed him and brought him in to form a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, do you know that you are the first person who says that Vukasinovic -- who says he saw Vukasinovic at the government session. Many people have been heard.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him for sure in Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you give statements with regard to the events we are discussing here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Borovic, asked you whether you had spoken to investigators from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when you spoke to them, and where?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Vukovar at the time they came to my house. It was related to the Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many people spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only the investigator, the interpreter and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was a statement compiled that concerned your interview?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. That was immediately after the war. It was a long time ago. I hadn't moved over to the other area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you try and remember the year, at least, when this took place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was before 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you shown a statement that had been drafted on the basis of your interview?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I think there was such a statement, but I can't remember exactly. It concerned the Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement of any kind, a statement that reflected the subjects you had discussed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I did sign such a statement, in that case I read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you saw Mr. Sljivancanin at the government session, and you said you were there very briefly. Tell me: Where did you see him, and what was he doing at the government session?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was with Vukasinovic. He was standing on the side when I saw him in the hall, when I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long was he there, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that was 15 years ago. I can't remember all the details. I don't know what sort of a belt he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, Your Honours. Mr. Jaksic, I can conclude something freely without insulting you. The Chamber is impartial. I won't say that you're lying, but I will say that you are not speaking the truth when you say that you could have seen Sljivancanin and Vukasinovic at the government session at the time that you are referring to, since there is evidence that shows that they were somewhere else at that time. Your testimony today, what you have said now at the end, is the result of your personal animosity that you bear against Mr. Sljivancanin, because you and your friends Milos Bibic, Boro Bugunovic, and Mile Uzenac were the subject of security and intelligence control, and you imagined that Mr. Sljivancanin was behind all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions, but I would like to hear your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one thing of putting a case to a witness. That was a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Do you have any comments on that, Mr. Jaksic, on what Mr. Bulatovic has just put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the gentleman's position and opinion. If that had been the case, five or six witnesses wouldn't have confirmed what I have said. I didn't have any contact with these witnesses. I didn't speak to any of these witnesses about that subject. I didn't prepare for this in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I don't know how it is that he knows what these witnesses said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what you said. I heard it from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jaksic. My name is Philip Weiner and I'm going to be asking you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- I'm going to be asking you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, okay? Sir, we were just talking about Major Sljivancanin, and you know that he served as the security chief for the Operations Group South and the Guards Motorised Brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you indicated in your testimony in Belgrade that he was in charge in the field or in the war operative zone. Do you recall testifying in the Belgrade court to that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin was in the field and he was in the position of the 1st -- the 1st Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you said, sir, that you felt that he was in charge in the field, that he would issue orders, that you obeyed his orders. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin was with Milivoje Bugunovic, in personal contact. I wasn't aware of that, but he personally cooperated with him. And he carried out operations on Milovo Brdo. Ask him who the Petrova Gora detachment was, the two companies, whether he was in charge of them, if he relieved me of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the Belgrade court, you said that you considered Major Sljivancanin as your superior. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how he acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if Mr. Weiner is talking about this witness's testimony from the Belgrade trial, could he provide us with the reference so that we can see where the relevant passage is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters are having a lot of trouble hearing Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On page 81 of your testimony in the Belgrade court, you said: "Since Sljivancanin was the Chief of Security of the Vukovar brigade, he was personally in charge of the war operative zone." Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the B/C/S version of the transcript which we have, you can't find this passage. Could we have the reference for the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. That is on page 0299-4638; and the ERN number, 02994638, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified, sir. Do you recall that testimony, since -- do you recall that, sir, testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if you go to page -- in the Belgrade transcript, 97, and I will have the cite for you in a second, sir. Page 97, in the B/C/S it is 02994650. You were asked about who your immediate superior was, and your answer is: "My immediate superior? Well, it depends. In the field it was Sljivancanin. Mrksic was his superior in the command. I attended meetings with Mrksic, although Sljivancanin was there as well, as well as others." Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, what is true? Did you consider Sljivancanin your immediate superior in the field, as you testified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never considered Sljivancanin to be my immediate superior, but, through his acts, he gave this impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's continue down on that same page. "Whose orders did you obey?" Your answer on that same page in B/C/S: "Mrksic's ones. Whatever has been agreed upon at the Operation Staff, Mrksic was the unquestioned authority, while Sljivancanin was, too, at that time in the field. It depended upon the situation." And you said: "Sljivancanin can also ..." and that statement ends there. Was that your testimony, and is that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if you go to the next page, page 98, you state -- that's the same page in B/C/S, page 98, you state that: "Sljivancanin was the one who could issue orders directly." That's right at the end of page 02994650, if you look at the B/C/S and those ERN numbers. You testified that Sljivancanin was the one who could issue orders directly. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know where Mr. Weiner found this in the transcript, where it says that this witness said that Sljivancanin could directly issue orders. In the transcript, in the part of the transcript mentioned by Mr. Weiner, you can find nothing of that kind. And this is the original B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the page 02994650, which is the seventy-first page of the statement in B/C/S. I have it highlighted right here. Right at the bottom you can see my highlighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can see the part of the text marked by Mr. Weiner, but could the exact text be read out in that case? Or Mr. Weiner should provide a copy of the B/C/S transcript so that the witness can read it out, so that he can read out what he said in front of the Belgrade court. The date of the transcript is the 28th of April, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He has it right in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page? Could you carry on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After that answer which you gave, Sljivancanin was -- I will give you the full answer: "Sljivancanin, Mrksic, was never at the battalion command here, but Sljivancanin was often there. Mrksic was in Negoslavci, and during the day, if there was room for an operations meeting to take place, we had it. If not, then in the field, during operations. Sljivancanin was the one who could issue orders directly." Do you recall saying that? And is that true?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin -- Mrksic's orders were the main thing for me. He couldn't order anything if it wasn't in accordance with Mrksic's orders. But with my company commanders, he often acted without me being aware of this, and he would also meddle with the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But when you said "Sljivancanin was the one who could issue orders directly," were you telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin could issue orders. Mr. Sljivancanin -- well, the battalions on the terrain were those who had authority. He could issue orders with regard to the security of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you said he was also meddling with your commanders, your own company commanders. Was he telling them what to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You testified, just a moment ago, that Sljivancanin was also meddling with your company commanders. Was he telling them what to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is footage or a recording that concerns the operation in the mini market. When they went to Milovo Brdo, Mr. Sljivancanin was with them. He was there instead of myself. As to whether he was in command, as to whether he was present, well, he should explain the situation himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I think we have reached the point where we must break. We will resume at 10 minutes past and continue then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one very short matter, before we start. We had the diary on its way to Belgrade today and we were setting up an appointment for someone to view it tomorrow. Now we're told that they would rather have it stay here and have someone examine it here. Can I get some official word as to what to do with the diary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The diary should come into the custody of the court officer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then parties can look at it under the supervision of the court officer. That would seem to be a practical arrangement, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. But it was requested to be in Belgrade for tomorrow, so I'm not going to release it to Belgrade tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I misunderstood you. I thought it was coming from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. It's here at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I better learn what the competing interests in it are. Can you help me, please, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. In complying with your ruling on the right of the Defence to inspect this diary of P002, we have been negotiating with the OTP to have this inspected. Up until yesterday we believed that the diary was in Belgrade. Yesterday, when we talked to the OTP, they informed us that the notebook or the diary was, in fact, here in the Tribunal's very building. It was for that reason that we requested to have the inspection carried out here, simply in order to save money, instead of having one from each of our teams sent back to Belgrade thereby incurring additional expenses. In addition to this, we have agreed to have both parties' experts present, which the Chamber agreed on some days ago. We shall be looking at the notebook, at the diary, and then following further consultation, we shall see what steps are best taken. And we'll be sure to inform the Chamber in due course of any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, just to make this perfectly clear, yes, it is true that this was scheduled for the following Saturday in Belgrade, an informal meeting but with the experts present. Mr. Moore said, "I don't believe I can arrange for my expert to be there." He was supposed to come back to us with some feedback, but he hasn't spoken to us since. What my learned friend has just said, all the teams can stay here and carry out the inspection. That is one thing. The other thing, the witness himself, P002 is in Belgrade. He can provide a sample of his handwriting, and it is on the basis of that that an inspection can be carried out for the diary to be sent to Belgrade, and for the experts to study the sample provided and the diary. I just wanted to add this to what my learned friend has already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weiner, it would appear at the moment that the diary should stay here, and that you or Mr. Moore needs to discuss the time at which your expert and the Defence expert would meet together and work on the matter. But it will be necessary for you to secure from the witness samples of his ordinary handwriting at some stage. Beyond that, I don't think I can usefully add or suggest anything at the moment. But above all else, it seems that any inspection needs to be here rather than Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll maintain the diary here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Weiner, your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir. I have one more question on this matter. And if you would look to the bottom of page 02994638, continuing into 4639 in your booklet, you gave an answer in Belgrade: "Since Sljivancanin was the Chief of Security of the Vukovar Brigade, he was personally in charge of the war operative zone. Mrksic was in the Operative Staff, which means the commander. He was in command," And then you have: "He was in the field all the time, and therefore he was kind -- a kind of undeniable authority. He took decisions. His decisions were indisputable. Then he said, 'Since Miroljub has proven himself to be a good fighter,' and I was already affected a bit by a Vietnamese syndrome, I had begun withdrawing into myself, I felt that I had difficulties in communication and the like, and then he said, 'Miroljub, you will be the commander of the Vukovar TO.'" Do you recall that testimony, sir, and do you recall that situation? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation. I'm not receiving any interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can. Now I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is, if you can, look at the book in front of you, at the bottom of page 02994638 into 4639. You can look at it. I can read it to you. It's the last tab.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: He has it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It is also on your screen. Your answer to a question in Belgrade was: "Sljivancanin was the Chief of Security of the Vukovar Brigade. He was personally in charge of the war operative zone. Mrksic was in the Operative Staff, which means the commander. He was in command, he was in the field all the time, and therefore he was a kind of undeniable authority. He took decisions. His decisions were indisputable. Then he said, 'Since Miroljub has proven himself to be a good fighter,' and I was already affected a bit by a Vietnamese syndrome, I had begun withdrawing into myself, I felt that I had difficulties in communication and the like, and then he said, 'Miroljub, you will be the commander of the Vukovar TO.' So then I stepped out." Now, do you recall that testimony and do you recall that situation, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph, you were speaking about both Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it was Sljivancanin that was in the field all the time.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you talk about the person who was in the field all the time, you said: "Therefore, he was a kind of undeniable authority. He took decisions. His decisions were indisputable." That's what you said about Sljivancanin. You're nodding your head. Can you ...

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unchallenged in the sense of freedom of movement, coming, going, security-wise, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said his decisions were indisputable. That's what you said; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it comes down to the same thing, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Your Honour, after he was shown a portion from his testimony, before the district court in Belgrade, the witness explained what sort of decisions he had in mind. The OTP now seem to be unhappy with this. They're trying to rephrase the question and trying to get the witness to say something which is contrary to what he originally said. And the witness specified this was only about security-related decisions, about freedom of movement, and he said exactly what it was that he had in mind when he used these words before the district court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. I leave it to you, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the record speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue, sir. Let's go to that time around November 16/17. Recall the day that you were at the 1st Assault Detachment when Sljivancanin, Tesic and Miroljub Vujevic was there. Do you recall that day, the day when there was a change in your command? Just as a start, do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that by chance in this notebook. On the 17th of November, I was at this meeting. I was at this meeting, preparations, what and how after the liberation of Vukovar. Meaning, if I was at the meeting of the 17th, and operations around Milovo Brdo were underway, then I wasn't anymore because -- the TO commander of Vukovar. But something else: The TO commander of Vukovar was for the town of Vukovar and the rest was supposed to start functioning with all the other villages, to be in touch and to establish some sort of a structure throughout the area. But Sljivancanin appointed Miroljub commander of Vukovar, and he just took over, without really knowing. He was now the commander of Operations Group South TO and the town of Vukovar, and I just withdrew and ceased to exercise any sort of duty whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it one step at a time. At that meeting -- just one more question. I just want to get who was there. We have had testimony in this Tribunal that Captain Radic was there. Do you recall him being at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend could please quote the relevant portion. Where did he get this from, that Captain Radic was there? Who said it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: P022, on day 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I will not be interrupting any more. Which is the date? Which particular circumstances did this witness address? I'm familiar with the statement, but that's a different context there, isn't it? So can the witness please have this shown to him. What were the circumstances? What was the date? We can't just have the name bandied about like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to ask him if he recalls --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic is concerned whether your reference is to the same meeting, on the same date as you are putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. It talks about Mr. Miroljub Vujevic was appointed TO commander at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That seems enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall - I know it's been a long time - but do you recall Captain Radic being at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any details. But now that I am here, I see what the real reasons were behind my removal at the time. I said that thing about the Vietnam syndrome.
