That may have been true, but that didn't necessarily affect my command or my staying there. I now see why Mr. Radic was so cress fallen at the command and why he didn't talk to me. I see why nobody worked with me or talked to me at the command. It is all Mr. Sljivancanin's fault. I simply didn't believe at the time that a security organ could have harassed or mistreated an officer like that, and have him removed deliberately on purpose and false accusations. And now I think counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin has revealed to us, finally, what the real situation was. And at the time I remember myself wondering why Mr. Radic was looking at me with such scorn whenever he came to the headquarters. That was on account of Mr. Sljivancanin, who failed to secure everything that he was supposed to. But he was certainly very good at ordering people about. So this must have been the reason. If he was an operative officer, then he should have been familiar with all of these. He should have known the reasons. He should have known what to do. Instead, he just used false information, misinformation, circulated by his -- by his subordinates, whereas my conscience was always clean and I had no blemish on my conscience. It's only now that I know the real reasons behind my removal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We will talk about the reasoning a little bit later, or on Monday, of your removal. You will get a chance to discuss that. I just want to go through the facts of the removal, which is -- very basically take you through and just go through those issues. And you will have a chance to discuss the basis either later today or Monday, all right? So at that meeting, just briefly, Mr. Sljivancanin relieved you of your command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't a meeting. It was the usual thing, coming to the headquarters. Miroljub was there, Mr. Tesic was there, I was there. He nudged him with his shoulder and said, "From now on, you are the TO commander. You are the man in charge," thereby relieving me of my duty. That wasn't a command meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you obey the order of Sljivancanin and accept the relief -- being relieved of your command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my information had come from the army security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had confidence in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- we will talk about that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I need to get the basics. Did you accept -- I just need some yes or no answers, and later we will get to all the reasoning, but right now, just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you accept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did Miroljub Vujevic obey Sljivancanin's order and accept the position? Did he obey the order?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could hardly wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never questioned Sljivancanin's authority at that time to relieve you and appoint someone else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only logical, because Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Mrksic were the two direct superiors, it was only logical he would trust him more than he would trust me, since we had just met for the very first time. I didn't want to press this. But there was another reason behind this. I had received word from the army's intelligence that there were plans to have me killed. I have four children, I have a family, and I simply didn't wish to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We will get to that. Don't worry. We have a long time to go. Now, when Sljivancanin relieved you and promoted Vujevic, he never said that he was acting on behalf of Mr. Mrksic, did he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sljivancanin never said he was acting pursuant to Mrksic's orders, did he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't confirm and he didn't deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, he never said that he was conveying anyone else's orders when Sljivancanin relieved you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, this had occurred right after Milovo Brdo was taken. So would you agree, basically once Milovo Brdo was taken, the battle of Vukovar was over. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said at the time. However, I have since found a notebook with the date written down and the place of this meeting. That was the 17th of September. And Milovo Brdo was taken on the 17th of September. So prior to the 17th of September - I wasn't there when Milovo Brdo was taken - I had been relieved of my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said "17th of September". Do you mean November?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. November, yes. Yes. November. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, since Milovo Brdo had been taken, all that was left was what you would call a bit of mopping up, you know, bits of work here and there, but the major battles was over. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. When Milovo Brdo was reached, control was established over both bridges. And as far as the Danube, the Croat paramilitary forces had been split up. Nikica and the downtown area, those were now too far apart. They realised what sort of situation they were facing and they called for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time you hadn't -- when you were relieved, we've got Milovo Brdo over, basically the battle is over. On September -- I'm sorry, November 17th, you hadn't committed any disciplinary violations requiring your removal.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. No. Actually I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You're certain, okay. And you also -- you hadn't committed any crimes requiring your removal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you hadn't disobeyed any orders requiring your removal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel has stated all the reasons, with great precision. He has clarified the matter himself, why I was removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that very shortly, sir. But you hadn't disobeyed any orders, correct, requiring that you should be removed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, in a situation where one feels humiliated, mistreated, not esteemed as a person, well, you can imagine what one must feel in that sort of situation. And that certainly was the case between me and Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I understand. But if we look at it, sir, at that time the battling was pretty much over. There was some mopping up, if you want to call it, that had to be done, finishing. There was no practical reason to remove you from that position. There was no need to dismiss you at that time. Wouldn't you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should ask Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you're not aware of any reason to dismiss you, for practical -- there is no practical reason to dismiss you at the time; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. No reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know, sir, having testified in Belgrade, that your successor Miroljub Vujevic was convicted for murders occurring just days after your dismissal. You're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as an experienced officer - you were a reserve captain - you would have not followed any orders to murder prisoners or civilians; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It is a tradition with the Serb army ever since the Balkan wars, that's what our training implied, that's what the principle of subordination implied. It was the Serb word of honour, and that is something that one always had to live by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And sir, being an experienced officer, you would not have ordered your subordinates or your soldiers to murder prisoners; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about Mr. Sljivancanin again. You've testified that you saw him at that meeting at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You've also testified that you saw Mr. Vukasinovic. What was his relationship or what position did he have in relation to Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was superior personally to the military police, a superior of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've testified that you were a security organ at some time after in the Republic of Srpska Krajina army, you were a security organ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was probably misrecorded. The chief of security of the brigade of Vukovar's TO, but that was before the war. That was a legal unit of the Vukovar TO, the brigade. But that was back in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, you know what a security organ or a security assistant does or the chief of security does, and with that knowledge of the type of work that person does, wouldn't you expect the Mr. Sljivancanin or one or more of his deputies to attend a meeting like the one at Velepromet? It wouldn't be unusual for a person in that position to attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is speculation. That's all my learned friend is doing. We've all heard the witness say he didn't know what was on the agenda at that particular meeting or what the meeting was about. What he could or could not have expected belongs purely to the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I would suggest you don't pursue that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you did see Mr. Sljivancanin and his deputy Mr. Vukasinovic at that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the room. In the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you could please draw Mr. Weiner's attention to the fact that he shouldn't misrepresent evidence. The witness never said he knew Vukasinovic to be Mr. Sljivancanin's deputy. He said Vukasinovic was in charge of the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Sljivancanin's deputy security organ, and that's what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was his testimony yesterday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you see Sljivancanin and Vukasinovic in that large hall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say specifically, but where the door is. But I remember them being there. I'm not sure if they were there throughout the meeting or not. Or maybe they just came at the beginning and left. But they certainly were in that hall when I came. I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were they together when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask you some questions in relation to Colonel Mrksic. You testified in Belgrade that you took orders from Mrksic and you obeyed orders from Mrksic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And on page B97 of the transcript, Belgrade, you referred to him as the "unquestioned authority". Was that true, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A much esteemed officer, always held in high regard by all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified -- or there was a situation where, in 19 -- sometime in 1991, I believe in the fall, you were appointed commander of the Operation Group South TO in Orolik?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The TO staff south.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orolik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were appointed by the civilian community to be the head of that TO staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerned 20 villages in the south and an operative zone. And the command of those villages were there because they all had units in those villages. And they had a meeting - I wasn't at the meeting; I was at the front line - and later I found out that they had elected me as the commander of that TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said Mrksic did not allow you to take that position; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me, "That's a political position. Vukovar has to be liberated -- first Vukovar has to be liberated and then we can pursue those policies."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you said Mrksic did not allow you to take that position; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't go to all the meetings; other people from the staff went. I only went to Lovac on one occasion, and I think I went to Ralik on one occasion. And there was a meeting on the 17th, a meeting they had requested in Velepromet. I think there were those three meetings, but it was over a short period of time, a one-month period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you said, and I'm quoting you, on page 81, which is 02994638 in the B/C/S, three-quarters of the way down the page on page 81: "Mrksic did not allow it." And just a very simple question: Mrksic did not allow you to take that position; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you followed and obeyed Mrksic's orders, isn't that correct, and did not take that position?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't officially take up that position, but later, at the request of others, I went to a meeting in Lovac and Ralik. I informed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't contest Mrksic's authority to tell you not to take that position.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I was in the command with the Petrova Gora detachment and with Tesic. I was there -- I spent more time there than in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. But the question is: You did not contest Mrksic's authority to tell you to refuse the position. You didn't contest his authority.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, I would like to talk about subordination. You discuss that in your statements -- in your statement of 2003 to the judge at Novi Sad, and you also discussed it in your testimony in Belgrade. And you indicated that the TO units in Vukovar were subordinated to the JNA. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution of the former Yugoslavia, the TO units were subordinated to the JNA. If the units didn't act independently in the field and if they were a part of the JNA, since the JNA was more equipped and more professional, if that was the case, it's a principle that these units would be under the JNA. But it what possible for the infantry battalion, for example, to be subordinated. But in this case, in this war, the reverse was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you explain that again, about the reverse being the case. It didn't get through the transcript. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the JNA is a more professional army, as a rule the Territorial Defence units would be under the JNA. But in the course of combat, a territorial battalion might be -- might have an armoured battalion under it. They would be under the TO officers if it was necessary for a given task. But in this war, the reverse was the case, the relationship between the TO and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand. But you also said the TO units, in your testimony in Belgrade, would be subordinated to a JNA unit that was in a particular area. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were subordinated to the Operative Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, in the fall of 1991 in Vukovar, all of the units, whether it was TO units, volunteers, detachments, these were all subordinated to the JNA, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to look at Exhibit 353, please. Can you see that in front of you? If they could make it a little clearer.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we look at page 2 in the English, which is page 1 in front of you, the second column, right side, there is a question. I believe it is the third question. It's on page 1 in the English, and it is: "Who were your soldiers?" And would you follow along as I read the next three sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my learned friend first put a question and then show the text, because this is leading. If he could first ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, this is cross-examination. You may put a document to the witness, but you will appreciate, as Mr. Borovic is implying, that there certainly will likely to be more reliability if it's done the other way, and the Chamber is likely to be more influenced by answers that haven't been immediately prompted by a written document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- with a view to assess whether you want to give emphasis as to weight or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you familiar with the size of Captain Radic's company?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise, but perhaps the witness shouldn't read the text. Perhaps he should answer the question without reading the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want it off the screen, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think it's too late. Maybe just let me do it the way I was going to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's read the first three sentences of the paragraph that I have referred to, the answer to the third question, which is: "Who is --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation) Your Honours, you were quite clear. Mr. Weiner is going back to a procedure that you have not allowed. I don't see why the witness should now read out something of this kind. But in any case, the witness has already been reading this text. But I think the Chamber should take into consideration the fact that my learned friend has been trying to get something in that shouldn't really be allowed, according to the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, could I just make something clear: In cross-examination, it is proper, it is allowed, to put a document to a witness and then to ask that question whether that reminds them, whether they agree with the document, or whatever. That can be done. The problem with that is that it's of less weight if the witness says, "Oh, yes, that's right, I agree, that's what happened," than if the witness does, as you suggested, that is speak about it first and then if something is overlooked, maybe he is able to remember it reading a document later. So your way is better, but this can still occur. We are well aware of what is happening. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you follow along. It states: "At one point there were about 500 people of different nationalities with different party affiliations --"

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall whether the companies in Vukovar were made up of various groups and various persons and persons from all different locations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Miroslav Vojinovic [as interpreted] and Radic, and he had a company of 120. This was the main direction, and all the forces that were mobilised, the TO and volunteers, were attached so that they could carry out that part of the task and head on to Milovo Brdo, because Mitnica was more fortified and it wasn't possible to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Everything is correct, but there is an error in the transcript. He said along the axis of action of Mr. Radic, there was Milorad Vujevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that could be corrected in the transcript. I think that the witness has done that himself. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And yesterday you were asked, while we're speaking of this, whether it was possible for a detachment to be subordinated to a battalion company. Do you remember that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And later I understood the gentleman's question, but I haven't clarified what happened to the detachment. He thought that I had subordinated the entire detachment to the company; however, on the 3rd of October, when the Guards Brigade launched an attack, I placed two companies into assault detachments, two companies in each detachment, in the 2nd Assault Company; and the other two companies, the 3rd and the 4th, while I was there with Major Bajic over the first two days, and my deputy, Cicak, was with Major Tesic. Since the commander of the 4th Company was killed on the 3rd, there were quite a lot of wounded and killed. On the 5th, the commander of the 2nd Company was killed. This was the fortified axis. You couldn't go there. We decided to head towards the left. I disbanded two companies. I gave ten soldiers to Zjajo. I subordinated a large group to the barracks, to guard the left wing of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Slow down. But what you're saying is, basically, during wartime, there has to be some flexibility; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Let me just clarify this with regard to Borovic's question. Two companies were disbanded. The soldiers were subordinated. The Galija [phoen] units, to the barracks; and some of them were guarding buildings. There was this protection platoon. Only two companies remained afterwards. In mid-October there were two companies, Miroljub's and Stanko's companies. I then moved to the command of Major Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, and Mr. Weiner. I would just like what the witness said to be in the transcript. Those two companies became part of the 1st Assault Detachment. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They cooperated with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- put them to me, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the witness said that those two companies, "I subordinated them to the 1st Assault Detachment." It is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they were cooperating with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my colleague clarify this matter, because that's what the witness said. That's what I heard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weiner --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- could you clarify that with the witness, if you would like? If not, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll be happy to. We'll take it one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You talked about Miroljub Vujevic, and you also spoke of Stanko Vojinovic. First, these people were not JNA company commanders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that they reported to JNA company commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to intervene. First, we haven't clarified the issue that concerns the 1st Assault Detachment. This is quite new. This is something the witness hasn't spoken about so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, Mr. Weiner is going to clarify a number of things, including that one, in an order that he thinks is sensible, so we will be patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You know who the -- oh, can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. At Tesic, at the command place, I had communications and Major Tesic had communications. He was in charge of his companies; I was in charge of my companies, until the end of the shift. I had a direct line with the company commanders from the front line. And at the first line, there was Miroljub's company, and Radic's company, and Stanko's company with Bojkovski's company. They were cooperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that they were cooperating. Let's take it one step at a time. You testified in Belgrade; page 117 in the English, page 02994663 in the B/C/S. 02994663. Now, do you recall being cross-examined at that time, during that time, by the accused in that case, Miroljub Vujevic? Do you recall that? And Miroljub Vujevic says to you, questions you: "How many of us transferred to the company of Radic? What was its strength? I don't know which of my 1st Company was. As far as I remember, you mentioned it there. So how many of my people were in my company?" And you answered: "At one point there were around 120, but that was at the end, because, as Vukovar was being liberated, the civilians who were freed immediately joined in. They were mobilised and assigned to companies to be attached. So it gradually became bigger as the end was nearing." Is that correct, that testimony that you gave in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They had 120, but from March they had 117, or on the 3rd. I have the list. On the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not March. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in that question, Miroljub Vujevic asked: "How many of us were transferred to the company of Captain Radic?" He asked you that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, everyone tries to appear innocent. He wanted to be subordinated to Mr. Radic so that he wasn't responsible. Perhaps later on, when I was replaced, maybe he was then subordinated to Mr. Radic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you never said at that time, sir, "You weren't subordinated to Radic."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't subordinated to Radic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you never said to Miroljub, "You weren't subordinated to Radic," when he asked that question.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never subordinated to Radic. He can say that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he did say that, that he was transferred to Radic in his question, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an order of Mr. Mrksic's dated the 3rd. According to that order, TO units had to be at the front line, even before the Guards Brigade, because they were familiar with the field and the situation and they could lead the action. So there was, so to speak, cooperation. They intermingled. But the command -- the chain of command was by me to my companies, and Tesic to his company. But they did cooperate in the field. They certainly cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we move to page 81, sir, which is 02994638, you say in the middle of the page: "Miroljub practically had his superior commander, and Stanko had his, who was commander of their company. He was immediately -- actually, the TO was subordinated to that command as well." That's what you answered.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I wasn't there, that was the case. When I was at a meeting, when I wasn't present, that was the case. I can't remain without a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So they were subordinated to JNA company commanders.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a certain sense, there was cooperation. So, yes, in a certain sense. It was an unwritten rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that there was a joint command post between Radic and Stanko -- and Vujevic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Joint command post of Radic and Vujevic, but it was in Stanko's house. His house was there. Stanko was to the right of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ever attend any meetings there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at a meeting there on one occasion, but they would come to the command as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you were aware that Radic held meetings there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Radic would discuss plans with his soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you also aware that Radic would sleep there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, could you move to page 120. I hope we don't have to move around as much as we go through the day. Now, you indicated, again, on page 120, which is 02994665 and 4666, you were asked -- one second, please. You were asked by Stanko Vujinovic: "Let me ask Mr. Jaksic one question. Does he know Sasa Bojkovski?" "Yes, I do." Question: "Do you know that I was in his company?" "DUSAN JAKSIC: Mr. Presiding Judge, I know that." So you knew that Stanko Vujinovic's unit was subordinated to Sasa Bojkovski, another JNA company commander. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that if I went to a meeting, if I wasn't present, then they would cooperate. But those where there were companies. Since they were more professional and they were more familiar with the situation, then you had to act with soldiers. As a result they cooperated with them directly. There was subordination to them, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There was subordination to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an important issue. That's why I'm intervening. To show parts of the transcript from the Belgrade court is allowed, but if the context is the question of Stanko Vujinovic for this witness, well, in that case, could the Prosecution continue with what he's doing and then we will have the answer that this witness provided to the court. It's not my right to examine now, so could my colleague, Mr. Weiner, say how Stanko Vujinovic decided and how Sasa Bojkovski decided? Could he ask questions so that we can establish this to show whether this was cooperation or subordination. If the remainder of the text is read out, it will be possible for the witness to answer the question completely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, part of the issue seems to be that your reference to Belgrade transcripts is not satisfactorily complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will continue reading. That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. And you haven't forgotten Mr. Borovic's earlier point, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will get to that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm glad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's get to that now. Sir, within your Petrova Gora detachment, you had four companies; then it became three companies. And those were, if you want to call it, detachment company --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Two, okay. And Miroslav Vujevic and Stanko Vujinovic were the two leaders of those companies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your full detachment was within the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I subordinated to the 2nd Assault Detachment, the part that remained, from those two subordinate companies. I subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. So they were divided among two assault detachments, your detachment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I might perhaps clarify, if I may, the question of subordination and all the rest. This was for as long as the line was there, the line of attack. That's what it's called. When Vukovar was liberated, I am asking you: Is it possible to have these compact units together? Everybody's in charge of their own unit; right? They had no command post of their own. They were available. I don't know what the subordination was at this point. You should ask someone else. You should ask, perhaps, Mr. Sljivancanin if he had subordinated Miroljub to Radic, or whether he was, in fact, independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were in charge of your unit, which was divided among two assault companies, the two major units, Miroslav's and Stanko's were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His detachment was not divided between two assault companies but, rather, two assault detachments. I think the question has been misphrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Among two assault detachments. But the two companies that you had, Miroljub's and Stanko's, were working with two JNA companies; isn't that correct?.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness's answer. Could the witness please be asked to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat that answer? The interpreters didn't hear it. The question was, again: Miroljub's and Stanko's companies were working with two JNA companies; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The large company, which was Miroljub's, was working with Radic's company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And Miroljub said that he was transferred to Radic's company, isn't that correct, when he said in Belgrade? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that means. Did Mr. Radic get an order to transfer or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Miroljub's company subordinated to Radic's company, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can my learned friend please stop pressuring the witness? The witness has said on a number of occasions that there was no subordination; rather, there was cooperation. He exercised command over Miroljub's company. And there was some heavy pressure exerted on the witness, despite the ten or so answers that were crystal clear. Well, there, perhaps the witness can be allowed to answer the question himself rather than be subjected to this sort of pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, it is cross-examination. I don't judge at the moment that it has gone too far. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Miroljub's company was subordinated to Radic's company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, two companies were subordinated to me and three companies to Major Tesic. Out of my two companies, I sent one to Radic and the other to Bojkovski. Zirovic had nothing with me. He had some volunteers that weren't under my command. I only had those two companies. When the operations in Vukovar were carried out, I used the radio to command my units, and Major Tesic, his own three units. Until the preparations ensued for Milovo Brdo and for Leva Supoderica, I was no longer in that post. And I don't know if they were later subordinated to anyone and what the orders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Vujevic, Miroljub Vujevic, received his orders from Radic -- received orders from Radic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were together at the same command. They drew maps and made plans. I know they made a plan for the code words for the attack. That was just before my shift. The attack on Milovo Brdo and Leva Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But do you know, sir, whether or not Miroljub Vujevic received orders from Radic? Do you know? If you don't know, that's fine. But do you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't. I don't know about my commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you sent Miroljub Vujevic's unit to Radic's company, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said already, there was an order from Commander Mrksic to send our companies, two down the axis of one assault attachment and two down the axis of the other, to out the scouts and work with them. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you did send them to work with Radic's unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the same line, the same attack, the same everything, and it was only logical for them to work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at Radic's statement in Exhibit 353, if you look at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know it's an exhibit, but we don't yet know whether this is Radic's interview, since he has not yet appeared as a witness and he's intending to. This is not Radic's evidence, so as not to mislead the witness. If it's an interview, well, I've nothing against this. Perhaps now that all of these questions have been asked would be the right moment to show this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an exhibit, and being an exhibit, the record speaks for itself, and I would like to use it and question him on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That portion that you read about 500 people of different nationalities and with different party affiliations in the company, "which I commanded. There were active service men, volunteers, reservists, Chetniks and Serbian volunteers. I had to unite them under one command to ensure success". In that statement, Mr. Radic is speaking about unity of command and that he was in charge of the people in his company from all the various groups; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that here Mr. Radic is referring to volunteers and Chetniks. I had no such units under my command. I only had Miroljub's company, and I know that there was an order from Mr. Mrksic to have them all together, the insignia and everything, that nobody was to stand out and everybody was to sport the same JNA insignia. It wasn't as if the Chetniks and those others and those yet others could afford to be different from anybody else. That was the gist of the order. If there was subordination to a JNA unit, then this subordinated unit had to sport JNA insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And if you have various units, you can only have one command, and that was JNA command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're subordinated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if they're working together, only one person can issue the orders. Under the doctrine of single command, you have one chain of command, and that was the JNA command in Vukovar in the fall of 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well, you're trying to get me to say that the TO unit was directly subordinated to a JNA unit. At the time, I wasn't a commander any more, the way you're phrasing your question. I did not have any power over these two companies, at least according to what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir -- excuse me. Sir, you testified in Belgrade that the TO was subordinated to a company, a JNA company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean? If it's not subordinated, the commander, who was not actually a reserve officer, would not have been entitled to do something that was outside the regulations governing command and governing orders. If, indeed, that had been the case, it was only to be expected that a JNA officer would have reacted. He was entitled, as an official, in the absence of a commander, to act. That is only normal, in as far as he was able to, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 81 in the English and 02994638 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand English, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. I've got the B/C/S page, the Serbian page. 02994638. Do you see the question from the presiding judge? You see: "Vujevic and Vojinovic deny, they say they were not commanders, company commanders." Your answer: "They were not because they were directly seconded to the Guards Company. Maybe that is why they say that. And the Guards Brigade, Mrksic requested that. Since we were local population, we should always be at the front line, and because we knew the area we should be at the front line, so that they -- and Miroljub practically had his superior commander, and Stanko had his -- who was the commander of their company, he was immediately, actually the TO was subordinated to that company as well."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no other command. In the absence of the TO commander, this subordination is logical. If I'm off to a staff meeting, needless to say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last portion of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When Miroljub's unit was at the front lines, fighting with Radic's unit, would you usually be with them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I go there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more frequently to Stanko's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So since you were not -- since you were less frequently at Miroljub's unit, someone had to command them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was -- well, I was -- countless times. I told Miroljub about the shortcomings and virtues of a commander. At the outset there were problems when heading into an operation. He couldn't start all over from scratch. For example, 7.00 they got the people altogether. I leave. He goes into action. And then he leads a squad instead of a company, and the others were not joining on this mission. And then I kept telling him what an officer should do. If you want to be a commander, in all the squads, all the platoons, you need to give everybody very specific assignments if you want to achieve any success at all. In this purely technical sense, he was probably aided by Radic later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after you left, the only one that was available to give him any commands was Radic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. This is something that you must ask Mr. Sljivancanin who appointed him, and if he left him there as a company commander, then he should know who he had subordinated him to, because I know nothing further about this. I can't tell you whether he was independent or whether he was, in fact, subordinated to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you aware of the Leva Supoderica unit in that area? Leva Supoderica unit.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Kameni's unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they weren't subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, they were also working together with Radic and Vujevic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, along the same axis, Leva Supoderica and Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not they were affiliated with any political party?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had something to do with the Radical Party, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was the party -- the Radical Party was the party of Seselj; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Seselj came to Vukovar and addressed the troops?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was in Vukovar, but I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see him while he was there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you hear him speak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was walking down Petrova Gora Street. He was at Petrova Gora as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you see him in the vicinity of that command post of Radic and Vujevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness never said Radic had a command post, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer then will be "no," Mr. Borovic, on at least that basis, if on no other. Carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at Stanko Vujinovic's house, which you testified was the joint command post of Vujevic and Radic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Command posts is where the commander is, and these were lower level commanders, the so-called komandiri. Therefore, it couldn't have been theirs. I saw his secretary there, a woman. I don't know what her name is, but she was the only one I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you said you saw her there --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She spoke something or other in that political party. But I didn't see in Stanko's house. I said I saw him as he was walking through Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you saw his secretary. Was that at Stanko's house?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. She was some sort of party member. I don't know her name exactly. I just saw her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said you saw her where? You said, "There". Where do you mean, "There"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Stanko's house, Stanko's house. I think it was nighttime already, late evening, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you testified about the meeting at Velepromet yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I have waited long, but you're moving off to quite a different topic now. Can we go back to the 3rd of October and sort out the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 3rd of October? You were in Vukovar, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of October, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at some time you moved in to Tesic's house.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose house?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tesic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tesic's?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post where Tesic was, the house where the command post was, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those two companies that I subordinated, and then I came to Tesic's command post because of those two companies. But that was sometime after the 5th. I don't know exactly, but it was certainly after the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, your detachment was subordinated as of October 3rd between two assault detachments; one was Tesic's and the other was the 2nd Assault Detachment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you mean. The detachments were on the Guards Brigade's payroll. This was something that was demanded at the meeting, and this was accepted. If I was subordinate to the commander of the Guards Brigade, well, this implies that the detachment, too, was subordinated to the Guards Brigade. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And within the Guards Brigade, they had three assault groups or companies. I'm sorry. Within the assault detachment, they had three companies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your men that were part of the -- part of Tesic's assault groups were split between the three companies; isn't that correct? Or two companies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two. Two companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the two companies that your men were split between were Radic's and Bojkovski's companies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bojkovski's, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that sufficient for the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since -- may I? Since there were three companies, so were these two. Two in the general area and the third in a narrower strip, which required no further manpower. And that's why only these two were split up. The third was only controlling a very small area. So one company was added to the first company, cooperating with the first company, and the second was cooperating with the second -- I'm sorry, with the third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the 3rd of October, you had four companies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I understand that you dealt with two of your companies by subordinating them to an assault detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Disbanded and resubordinated the soldiers to the assault detachment, because I had lost my commanders and I had a shortage of men. There had been losses, there were fewer men left, so I did some resubordination; ten of them to the special platoon. At the front line I resubordinated the rest of them. And then on the right flank, the TO manpower was required, those who knew the area, to protect the right flank. I left a rather large group there and had them resubordinated. And then I took the two companies and I went straight over to the 1st Assault Detachment. Between the 3rd and the 5th, I was with the 2nd Assault Detachment with Major Bajic, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the name of the major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bajic. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that you took two of your companies to the 1st Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second, the 2nd detachment. Extinguished and resubordinated the men to the 2nd Detachment. Since there was no command personnel, and for their needs, I subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, does that answer your concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most certainly, Your Honour, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just my own question. So you sent two companies to the 2nd Detachment, and two to the 1st?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few members. The 4th had 45; the 2nd, 72. There were a lot of losses. On the 3rd, the commander of the 4th Company was killed. On the 3rd, Pajic died. As I didn't have commanders, the company was disbanded, I resubordinated the remaining men to the 2nd Assault Detachment, and I also resubordinated men for the barracks security. Then I moved to the command of Tesic with the other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talked about the meeting in Velepromet. And you indicated that you only have a partial memory, you don't have all the facts. You don't recall all of the facts; you recall general substance. But exact times, exact places, you don't recall; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any duties or obligations, so it wasn't my duty to be there as a member of the government, at the session. Perhaps I spoke to people I knew outside of the hall as well. I didn't attend the entire session. If I had had any information, it would have been written down in my notebook. I didn't keep a record. If I had, I would have produced it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. You have no notes, you have no records or calendar of that meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take any notes, so I can't remember. But as for these events, it was only when I had a look at my notebook that I saw that on the 17th of November I attended that meeting, and I was able to read about the matters that were discussed, and about the deliberation of Vukovar, et cetera. I have the schedule of the company, the cooperation, commanders of the brigades, which directions, which axes were taken, how many men were involved. I have this all written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have this book with you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got this on me. It's in my room. In my first statement, 15 years have passed since then. I didn't know Pajic at the time, so I said that I had three companies. But I remember Fot, in fact. I knew him from before the war. So it was only when I saw or had a look at my notebook that I was able to present the facts such as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, would you be willing to make this notebook available, so someone could look at it, possibly the registrar could copy it, over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not? Why not? Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regard to the meeting at Velepromet, which you said is on --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But just a minute, if I may add something for the Judges. This notebook, well, there's a part that concerns the period from the 3rd of October to the 17th, and then I have another part that concerns the men wounded and killed, and then there is another part that concerns my time in the corps. I wouldn't want you to be confused. I used that very same notebook when I later worked as an officer in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could someone from the Victims and Witnesses Unit or Registry please see him in this weekend and try to facilitate a copying of that notebook for all parties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think at the end of this sitting, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Someone could go to my room now. I will provide the key and that book can be brought here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will be adjourning quite soon. I was going to say that we will arrange for a court officer to go with you to your room and obtain the notebook straight away and it can then be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will hand the handbook over. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have any notes -- you talk about the November 17th meeting when you were -- when Major Sljivancanin relieve you of duty. Do you have any notes relating to the November 20th meeting at Velepromet, in that notebook, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have some notes, but they only concern the 26th, from the 26th. I would have to have a look. I have the dates there. It's quite by chance that I found that notebook. I certainly had a smaller notebook, but since this one was a big notebook, that is probably the reason for which I didn't use it that often. I didn't often have it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you keep any notes of your meeting with Mrksic? Did you keep any notes, records --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an order in that notebook dated the 3rd of October, and perhaps even the 5th. Only those two. I didn't record anything else in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have no notes as to the meeting with Colonel Mrksic which -- when you went there at the request of Goran Hadzic? You have no notes about that, indicating times --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Goran Hadzic. Mr. Vojinovic. Not Hadzic, Mr. Vojinovic. No, I haven't. This was all done orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you went to see Mrksic, and then you returned to the meeting. In Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In Belgrade, you previously testified that you finished meeting with Mrksic. You then went to the barracks and saw Miroljub Vujevic and Stanko Vujinovic outside at the gate. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably when I also asked about Vukaric's [phoen] son. I probably noticed them on the road, in front of the KPS, before the barracks. I probably noticed those two people. I then stopped the vehicle. I said that I had seen Mrksic, and I told them about our request and about the decision that had been taken, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that after you had told Vujevic and Vojinovic, they became very upset over Mrksic's decision. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were disgusted; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In fact, you said they were "seeing red." That was in your statement to the investigative judge. You said that they were "seeing red". Do you mean that they were infuriated, really upset?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a certain sense, they were upset. They protested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you said at the same time you're talking to Vujevic and Vojinovic, the busses with the civilians were there at the barracks. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were the busses there. The civilians were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you then state in your 2003 testimony that you didn't stay long with Vujevic and Vojinovic, "and I left and went home." I'm reading your --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "I did not stay long, and I left and went home".

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just remember that I met them, I conveyed this information to them, and that was it. I didn't linger there. I don't know whether I went home. I don't know what I did. But I only remember that I was with them very briefly and just conveyed this information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said, "I don't know if I went home or what I did." So did you do some -- is it possible you did something --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JAKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. All I remember is that I saw them on my way. I stopped. I said that I had seen Mrksic, that we had requested that criminals be tried in our area. I conveyed that order. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is an error in the transcript and that is why Mr. Weiner is putting such a question. Page 82, line 6, the witness says, "I don't know whether I went home or to Velepromet," and that hasn't been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think that is clarifying the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. I'm going to have to ask you to continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know the information we have is that Mr. Vasic, who is not feeling well, has seen the doctor, he is feeling better, but he's been advised to rest this afternoon. And that's the situation as we know it. Now, Mr. Domazet, after this witness on Monday, do we have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The witness Milosevic is in The Hague. As far as I know, Mr. Vasic has already spoken to him and he is preparing for the witness to start today. But after the witness Jaksic we will have the witness Milosevic. He is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know you want to rush, but just two questions. One is, we have Milosevic on Monday, and I got the -- I had the impression yesterday that their next witness isn't coming till Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we have interruptions in witnesses this coming week, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness who was supposed to arrive with Milosevic had a heart attack and is now in hospital, the witness Lesanovic is the next witness who is to appear. But unfortunately it looks like he won't be appearing until Wednesday. And we also know that attempts are being made with regard to witness Milosevic, who has been subpoenaed, and attempts are being made for him to come, too. But at this point in time I'm not sure what to say. Perhaps we won't have a witness on Tuesday, if we conclude the testimony or complete the testimony of these witnesses on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's Milosevic and then Osamovic. We must now adjourn. I must ask you, sir, to return on Monday. And we will sit on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
